transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-16
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Ava Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Marconi (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Luxora Head of ML), Marcello Ortiz (Luxora Infra), Sami Reynolds (Product)
Shared: Optimize playbook deck (https://redwood.app/optimize/playbook/rt-prefetch), sample traffic link (customer provided: https://drive.luxora.com/sample_traffic.csv)

Auto-summary (auto): demonstrate Optimize recommendations for batching and KV prefix prefetch with cost sims across three traffic shapes.

[00:00] Ava: okay everyone thanks for joining, quick intros, I'm Ava from Redwood, together with Diego our SE. Luxora team, want to introduce?
[00:08] Priya: yes hi, Priya, head of ML at Luxora. we've been building sessionized customer chat, about 60k DAU right now, peak concurrency around 250, average turn length ~80 tokens.
[00:18] Marcello: Marcello infra, running on a mixed cloud, we have private VPC constraints and KMS for keys.
[00:25] Diego: awesome, thanks. Today I want to show Optimize console recommendations: batching windows, runtime batching, and an approach for prefix / KV prefetch that we call lookahead prefetch. We'll walk cost sims.
[00:37] Sami: quick ask — latency SLO is 200ms p50 for short responses, p95 can be 650ms but prefer <500.
[00:45] Diego: noted, that'll drive where we set batching windows and fallback rules.

[01:00] Diego: first slide — baseline. you said avg post-token length 80 incoming, response 150 tokens, so round trip ~230 tokens per request. At 60k DAU with 3 sessions per user per day that's ~540k requests daily.
[01:18] Priya: that estimate is a bit high for us cause lots of sessions are short, but rough is fine.
[01:26] Diego: cool. Scenario A (low concurrency): median batch sizes of 1.3 tokens per step, i mean 1.3 requests per batch when window is tiny; Scenario B (mid): 3.5 requests/batch at 40ms window; Scenario C (high): 7–10 requests/batch at 80ms window. That maps to token-per-second reduction and cost.
[01:50] Ava: note these micro-batches are continuous batching in the runtime, not naive queueing that raises latency too much.

[02:10] Diego: Now prefix / KV cache. There's two approaches: session prefix caching where we store the last N tokens per user (prefix) vs K-V lookahead prefetch where we precompute likely KV states for top N intents. For Luxora, with structured flows, we expect 45–65% prefix hit rate with a 2-day session TTL; lookahead prefetch to hit on 20–30% of calls but each hit can avoid 80–120 tokens of decode.
[02:42] Marcello: how expensive is memory for KV? we don't want GPU pinned memory blowing up.
[02:48] Diego: good question — runtime uses compressed KV (quantized / chunked) and we can offload cold KV store to host memory with async prefetch. Operationally you'd pick a hotset size — for your 60k DAU we recommended a hotset of 6k active sessions in-GPU, rest in node memory. That reduces GPU memory by ~60% vs caching everything.
[03:12] Priya: what's the estimate on token savings?
[03:15] Diego: in our sim, with prefix hits of 50% and lookahead adds 25% additional effective hits, we reduce decode tokens by ~55% overall. So if baseline is 230 tokens/request average, effective moving average drops to ~104 tokens. That cuts monthly token bill almost in half.

[03:38] Sami: numbers — can you show actual $ estimate?
[03:41] Diego: yes — rough hosted cost model: assume $10 per million input+output tokens (round number for demo). Baseline 540k requests * 230 tokens = ~124.2M tokens/day ~3.7B tokens/month -> ~$37k/mo. With caching and batching savings (55% token reduction + 25% further batching efficiency) you get to ~40% of baseline token spend => ~$14.8k/mo. Also batching reduces compute overhead which reduces effective GPU instance-hours — we show both lines in the spreadsheet.
[04:12] Priya: that delta is interesting. what's the latency impact at p95?
[04:16] Diego: depends. mid scenario with 40ms batching window adds ~40–80ms tail for queued requests, but big wins on throughput reduce queuing spikes in busy tails. Prefetch hits reduce decode time by up to 200ms because we skip early layers when k-v resumes. Net p95 in our mid sim stays under 500ms.

[04:38] Marcello: security. how do we handle KMS and keys for cached entries? we can't have plaintext session context in shared GPU.
[04:44] Diego: good — Redwood Private supports encrypting at rest and in-transit; KV entries are encrypted with customer-managed KMS keys. For private deployments we can keep KV store within your VPC, and use HSM/KMS for zero-trust. We will share SOC2 and KMS docs (link: https://redwood.app/security/soc2 and our ksm integration notes).

[05:05] Ava: quick demo time. I'm going to pull up the Optimize console.
[05:12] [screen share noise]
[05:20] Diego: Here is recommendations tab — workloads profile auto-detected. we show token histogram, concurrency heatmap, and recommended batching window with estimated savings. For your profile optimize suggests: 40ms window, hotset size 6k sessions, prefix TTL 48 hours, lookahead set to top 12 intents.
[05:40] Priya: how does the console calculate 'top intents'?
[05:43] Diego: we use clustering on canonicalized prompts + session goals; you can opt in to upload labeled intents or let the runtime infer. It shows expected hit rate and confidence bands.

[06:02] Diego: Now the simulator — we can toggle traffic shape from bursty to uniform, and see cost / latency curves. I'm switching to a bursty weekend scenario — notice p95 spikes if batching window is 80ms without autoscale. If we add autoscale and fallback to smaller model variants on overflow, tail is controlled.
[06:26] Marcello: fallback to smaller model — what about quality regression?
[06:30] Diego: we have model variant scoring in the console: you can set thresholds where fallback is allowed (e.g., only for diagnostic prompts or when latency > X). Also can route only non-sensitive sessions to lower-cost variants.

[06:45] Priya: can we test this on our own cluster? we run some workloads on-prem for compliance reasons.
[06:49] Diego: absolutely — Redwood Private supports an on-prem package. For pilot we recommend a hybrid: control plane hosted, inference in your VPC. That allows us to push caching and prefetch policies while keys and KV remain under your control.

[07:05] Sami: question about infrastructure: what are network egress assumptions?
[07:08] Diego: If inference runs in your VPC, egress is internal. For hosted inference, we estimate around 2–10% overhead due to sidecar/telemetry egress depending on logging level; we can throttle telemetry.

[07:28] Ava: want to walk through a concrete batch timing example. Diego?
[07:31] Diego: sure. Example: 100 RPS sustained, without batching each request triggers a separate decode; with 40ms window we coalesce about 4–5 requests per batch at that RPS leading to 60% reduction in model invocations. Combined with prefix hits you get multiplicative gains. The console shows time series and expected GPU utilization curves.

[07:58] Priya: are there risks where batching worsens UX (people notice delay)?
[08:02] Diego: yes for single-turn critical flows. We recommend no batching on high-priority endpoints (checkout flows, auth) and enable batching on exploratory chat and background recommendations. The route-level controls are in the Console — you can tag endpoints.

[08:20] Marcello: anything we need to instrument on our side before pilot?
[08:24] Diego: sample traffic profile (we need timestamps, session id, tokens in/out), list of endpoints and SLOs, and access to a staging VPC for infra team. Also a small secrets exchange for KMS provisioning.

[08:38] Priya: timeline — how quickly can we see results?
[08:41] Ava: Pilot can start within 7–10 business days once we have staging access and sample logs; 2-week run to gather stable hit rates. Diego will share the spreadsheet with scenarios.

[09:00] [longer discussion — customers ask about specific math and Diego steps through spreadsheet rows, muted audio in recording — transcription lower quality here]

[12:30] Diego: I want to highlight three conservative numbers in the spreadsheet: conservative hit-rate (30% prefix), expected hit-rate (50%), and optimistic (70%). Each maps to different monthly savings. We also show sensitivity to average response length — if average response drops to 100 tokens the absolute $ savings decline but % savings similar.

[15:05] Sami: competitor question — InferEdge claimed multi-tenant KV caching that keeps everything in GPU memory with smaller quant. How is Redwood different?
[15:12] Diego: Redwood focuses on a hybrid hotset + host-backed KV to balance memory and cost. Aggressively pinning everything on GPU increases instance counts and cost in many cases. Our approach recommends hotset sizing based on tail analytics.

[17:52] Priya: okay last big question — what about model updates and rolling hot KV? if we change model weights the KV format may change.
[17:58] Diego: good catch. the runtime supports KV format migration and version vectors; we recommend a canary migration where we warm new KVs for a subset of sessions and backfill during low traffic windows. Console has a migration plan generator.

[19:10] Ava: let's recap next steps and owners.
[19:14] Priya: quick note on compliance — we will need SOC2 docs and KMS integration details before infra approves pilot.
[19:20] Ava: we'll send those today. Diego: you'll take the cost sims, run three scenarios and attach to CRM. Marcello: provide staging VPC information and decide on preferred KMS (CloudKMS or other). Priya: send sample traffic.

[19:35] Diego: I'll put the three scenario sheets in the shared folder: https://redwood.app/shared/luxora-cost-sim. Those include the assumptions and raw math.

[19:45] Marcello: timeframe for pilot start? after we get docs we'll need 2–3 days to open staging.

[19:50] Ava: OK target pilot kickoff week of 2027-08-23.

[20:00] [closing pleasantries and small talk]
[20:12] Priya: thanks everyone — good session.
[20:15] Ava: thanks — we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and SOC2 pack.

[20:20] End of recording — rest of the meeting was wrap and scheduling details (not transcribed fully due to recording glitch).

Notes on transcription quality: there are segments with background noise and a 30s gap where the screen-share audio overridden the mic; some proper nouns (Luxora infra modules, Redwood Optimize internals) may be slightly misheard.
